bullets: How charge flows around one unbroken loop, why the current is the same everywhere in series, and how voltage, current and resistance are tied together by Ohm's law
slides.heading: Electricity: circuits, current and Ohm's law
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build one loop, follow the current around it, split it into branches, and finish with the law that ties voltage to current.

bullets: Describe a simple circuit and state the direction of conventional current
Compare series and parallel circuits and use Ohm's law, V = I R, to calculate current
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: The bulb glows brightly and gets hot, so it looks as if it is swallowing the electricity flowing through it
So is the current smaller after the bulb than before it - or exactly the same?
slides.heading: Does the bulb drink the current?
slides.notes: Ask for predictions and take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: the two-ammeter scene will settle it.

bullets: A circuit is one unbroken loop; conventional current flows from positive to negative; series gives charge one path and parallel gives it branches
Voltage, current and resistance obey V = I R: change one and the others respond - with resistance fixed, doubling the voltage doubles the current
slides.heading: Loops, paths and Ohm's law
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the map for the whole lesson: first the loop, then the direction, then the paths, then the law.

bullets: A circuit is one unbroken loop: the battery pushes charge around it, the bulb turns electrical energy into light, and the ammeter measures the flow
Break the loop anywhere and everything stops - there is no second route for the charge
slides.heading: A simple circuit
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: trace the loop with a finger, name each part as it appears, and stress that the loop is unbroken.

bullets: Conventional current leaves the battery's positive terminal, travels around the loop, and returns to the negative terminal
The red markers crawl along the wires in that direction - follow them, not the electrons
slides.heading: Conventional current flows + to −
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: follow the red markers out of the positive terminal and all the way back to the negative.

bullets: In series there is only one path, so one broken bulb kills the whole loop
In parallel each bulb sits on its own branch, so one can fail and the other stays lit
slides.heading: Series or parallel?
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: first the single series path failing as one, then the parallel branches surviving independently.

bullets: The battery steps from 6 to 12 volts with resistance fixed at 4 ohms, and the ammeter climbs from 1.5 to 3 amps
Check it with the triangle: V = I x R, so 12 divided by 4 gives 3 amps
slides.heading: Ohm's law: V = IR
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: watch the dial step up, the markers speed up, and the ammeter climb from 1.5 to 3 amps.

bullets: Put an ammeter before the bulb or after it - in a series loop every meter reads the same 0.5 amps
The bulb turns electrical energy into light and heat, but the current flowing out equals the current flowing in
slides.heading: Current is not "used up"
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: read both ammeters aloud - 0.5 amps before the bulb, 0.5 amps after it - and ask where any current could have gone.

bullets: Carry away three things: current flows from positive to negative around a single loop, series means one path while parallel means many, and in a series loop the current is identical everywhere, tied together by V = I R
slides.heading: Electricity in one minute
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: tick off the three takeaways as each one is restated, and point back to the scene that proved it.

bullets: V = I x R, so I = V / R = 12 / 4 = 3 A for the 12-volt battery across 4 ohms
Halve the battery to 6 V and the current halves too: I = 6 / 4 = 1.5 A - exactly what the ammeter showed
slides.heading: Worked example: Ohm's law
slides.notes: Work this on the board slowly: write the triangle first, then cover the I and read off V over R for both voltages.

bullets: A 9 V battery drives a 3 ohm resistor - find the current, then say what happens to it if the resistance doubles
Then open the worksheet: one circuit question, one used-up trap, one Ohm's law calculation and a series-parallel comparison
slides.heading: Your turn
slides.notes: Give three quiet minutes for the first task, take answers from the class, then set the worksheet going in pairs.

bullets: Four questions: the used-up current trap, an Ohm's law calculation, series versus parallel, and the direction of conventional current
Write one sentence: why does an ammeter read the same before and after a bulb in a series loop?
slides.heading: Exit ticket
slides.notes: Collect the tickets at the door; the first question revisits the trap head-on, so it shows straight away who still thinks the bulb drinks the current.
